posts.title: The 94% Stat
posts.text:
Here's a number most CEOs haven't seen yet: over 94% of webpages get zero traffic from Google or AI.

Not "a little." Zero.

They were never indexed, got buried under stronger competitors, or were judged too generic for AI to recommend.

Here's why that matters now: your buyers aren't just Googling anymore. They're asking ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude who they should trust. If AI doesn't know your company, you're not losing the comparison — you're not even in it.

The fix isn't more content. It's content AI can verify and cite.

Learn how AI decides to trust, cite, and recommend you.

posts.title: Search Gave 10 Options. AI Picks 1.
posts.text:
For 20 years, getting found meant ranking on page one. Ten blue links. Ten chances.

AI changed the math. When a buyer asks "who's the best ___" they don't get ten options. They get one answer. Maybe two.

Whoever gets recommended by AI gets the lion's share of the market.

The companies winning this space right now aren't the biggest. They're those whose expertise, proof, and structure are designed to gain AI's trust.

Learn how AI decides to trust, cite, and recommend you.

https://BehindTheCurtain.ai/10ThingsAILooksFor?utm_source=linkedin&utm_medium=group&utm_campaign={{utm}}

posts.title: Your Old SEO Content Is Now a Liability
posts.text:
An uncomfortable truth: the content that got you ranked on Google may be actively hurting you with AI.

Content built for the old playbook — keyword volume, templated articles, outsourced filler — doesn't just get ignored by AI. It can get flagged as suspicious. Why? Because too much of it is fake and AI sees it for what it is.

AI doesn't reward volume. It rewards companies it can trust, verify, and recommend with confidence.

So before you write another 20 blog posts, it's worth asking: am I building trust, or am I building noise?

Learn how AI decides to trust, cite, and recommend you.

posts.title: SEO vs. AEO vs. GEO vs. What Actually Matters
posts.text:
Quick translation guide, because the acronyms are getting out of hand:

SEO helps you get found. AEO helps you get answered. GEO helps you get mentioned.

None of those is the goal. The goal is to get CHOSEN.

Getting mentioned in an AI answer alongside four competitors is a participation trophy. Getting named as the one to call — that's revenue.

The discipline behind that is what we call Trust Engineering: turning expert copy, proof, and structure into the confidence Google, AI, and buyers need to pick you.

posts.title: The First Search Reset in 27 Years
posts.text:
If you've ever said "I wish I'd bought that domain in 1999" or "I wish I'd started on Google Ads when clicks were a nickel" — pay attention.

For the first time in 27 years, search is resetting. The rules that decided who gets found are being rewritten by AI, right now.

Resets are when small, fast companies take positions from big, slow ones. Your bigger competitors are carrying years of content built for rules that no longer apply. That's not an asset. That's baggage.

The window closes when the category hardens. In a year, you'll either say "I'm glad I did" or "I wish I had."

posts.title: Pre-Sold Prospects
posts.text:
When AI recommends you by name, the prospect arrives pre-sold — they've already been told you're the one to trust, before your sales team ever hears their name.

Compare that to a Google click: a skeptic comparing you against ten tabs.

Building that position isn't luck. It's engineering trust: structuring your expertise and proof so AI can verify it and cite it confidently.

posts.title: Ask AI About Your Company (A 60-Second Test)
posts.text:
Do this right now. It takes 60 seconds.

Open ChatGPT (or Claude, or Gemini) and ask: "Who are the most trusted [your category] companies for [your ideal client]?"

Three outcomes:

You're named confidently. Congratulations. Now you must defend it.

You're mentioned vaguely or with hedging. You're vulnerable.

You're not there at all. To AI-assisted buyers, you don't exist.

Most businesses who run this test for the first time get outcome #3 and then notice a smaller competitor sitting in outcome #1.

Learn how AI decides to trust, cite, and recommend you.

posts.title: Being Big Won't Save Them
posts.text:
A counterintuitive thing about the AI search shift: size isn't an advantage. It's often a liability.

Big competitors are carrying a decade of content built for the old rules — keyword-stuffed, templated, optimized for an algorithm that's being replaced. AI looks at that and sees noise, not authority.

A smaller company with expertise, verifiable proof, and consistent trust signals can take the trusted position before anyone even notices the game changed.

This has happened in every platform shift. It's happening again. The question is which side of it you're on.

posts.title: Trust Is Now Mandatory
posts.text:
"Trust" used to be a soft word. Branding. Vibes.

Not anymore. To an AI model deciding who to recommend, trust is a technical requirement: Can your claims be verified? Is your expertise demonstrated or just asserted? Is your proof structured in a way machines can read? Do independent sources corroborate you?

Anyone can claim authority. Our proprietary trust strategy makes it verifiable.

That's the whole shift in one sentence: marketing used to be about persuading people. Now it's about being verifiable to the machines people ask.

posts.title: One or Two Companies Per Market
posts.text:
Here's a market dynamic most people haven't thought through yet.

In old search, ten companies could share page one. In AI search, the recommendation usually goes to one name. The position isn't shared — it's owned.

Which means this is a land grab, and it's winner-take-most. Once a company in your category locks in the trusted position, dislodging them gets exponentially harder, because AI's confidence compounds with citations and time.

Someone is going to spend the time and money to own your category. The only open question is whether it's you or the competitor you like least.

posts.title: Why Your Content Calendar Isn't Working
posts.text:
You're publishing weekly. Traffic's flat. Leads aren't coming. Sound familiar?

The problem usually isn't effort. It's that the content was built to rank, not to be extracted and cited.

AI systems pull answers from content they can trust: clear expertise, structured claims, verifiable proof. Generic "5 Tips" posts give them nothing to extract and nothing to verify — so they pull from your competitor instead.

More volume won't fix a structural problem. Different architecture will.

posts.title: The Buyer Journey Changed While You Weren't Looking
posts.text:
The 2020 buyer: Googles the category → opens 8 tabs → builds a shortlist → calls 3 companies.

The 2026 buyer: asks AI "who should I trust for X" → gets one or two names → checks them out → calls one.

Notice what disappeared: the shortlist. The comparison phase. The part of the funnel where you used to win deals with a better website and a faster follow-up.

If you're not the name AI gives, you're not late in the funnel — you're outside it entirely.

posts.title: What AI Flags as Suspicious
posts.text:
Few people know this: AI doesn't just ignore weak content. It penalizes the patterns.

Templated articles. Outsourced filler. Keyword-stuffed pages. The exact tactics that worked in 2015 now read as signals of a company trying to look authoritative rather than being authoritative.

It's the difference between a resume full of buzzwords and a resume full of results. AI has gotten very good at telling them apart.

The companies getting recommended publish less, prove more, and structure everything for verification.

posts.title: The Question Behind Every AI Answer
posts.text:
When a buyer asks ChatGPT "who should I hire for X," the model is silently answering a different question: "who can I recommend without being wrong?"

AI systems are built to avoid confidently recommending something they can't back up. So they default to the companies whose expertise is documented, whose claims check out, and whose proof appears in multiple places.

That's the bar now. Not "best marketing." Not "most content." Lowest risk to recommend.

You can engineer your way to that position deliberately — or hope it happens by accident.

posts.title: Glad I Did vs. Wish I Had
posts.text:
Every platform shift produces two groups of founders.

Group one moved while it was early, unproven, and slightly uncomfortable. They own the positions now.

Group two waited for proof. By the time proof arrived, the positions were taken, and the price of entry had 10x'd.

AI search is at that exact fork right now. The data is clear (94% of pages get zero traffic from Google or AI), buyer behavior has already moved, and most categories still don't have an owner.

Twelve months from now you'll be in one of those two groups. Pick deliberately.

posts.title: Why Companies Are Adjusting to AI Search
posts.text:
Honest question for the room: how much of your marketing budget is still optimizing for 2019 Google?

Rankings, keywords, domain authority, backlink counts — all metrics from a system that's being displaced by AI answers in real time.

I'm not saying SEO is worthless. It's table stakes — included, but no longer the product. The product is being the company AI cites, ranks, and recommends.

Budgets follow habits, and habits lag reality by years. The founders who reallocate first take the position.

posts.title: Authority You Own vs. Paying For Ads
posts.text:
Ads stop the moment you stop paying. Rankings vanish with the next algorithm update. Social reach belongs to the platform.

A trust position with AI is different. Once your company is the verified, cited, recommended name in your category, that content compounds — and it's yours. Built once, working every time a buyer asks the question.

That's the most underrated part of this shift: it's the first chance in decades to build a demand asset you actually own instead of rent.

Ten years of content built for old Google isn't a moat — it's ten years of material AI reads as outdated, templated, and untrustworthy.

Everyone starts near the line. The advantage goes to whoever can get ahead and stay ahead.

posts.title: The Only Question That Matters in 2026
posts.text:
Forget rankings. Forget impressions. Forget follower counts.

One question decides who gets the inbound in your category this year:

When your ideal buyer asks AI who to trust, does it say your name?

If yes, protect that position — because someone is coming for it. If no, every day that stays true, the call goes to someone else.

You don't have to be the biggest company in your market. You have to be the easiest one for buyers, Google, and AI to trust. That's buildable.
